title: Pragmatism
author: William James
public_title: Why Decisive Choices Calm Your Brain Part 2 🧠
hook: You hesitate when picking a simple dinner spot.

sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You hesitate when picking a simple dinner spot. Overthinking small choices actually drains your mental stamina for hours. In 1998, psychologist Roy Baumeister at Case Western Reserve University measured how decision making wears down human willpower. In his study, about 67 participants forced to make tough choices gave up on later puzzles twice as fast as those who did not. In 1907, philosopher William James published Pragmatism. He argued that truth is simply what works practically in your daily life. He believed holding onto useless debates creates unnecessary internal friction. But does endless analyzing actually help you find the right answer? Modern brain scans show that prolonged overthinking triggers stress pathways instead of clarity. The result? Making a quick, workable choice yields better mental health than searching for perfection. That is it. So why do we assume endless analyzing leads to better outcomes? Because our minds confuse hesitation with careful thought. So next time you freeze, remember you hesitate when picking a simple dinner spot.

claims.claim: Making decisions depletes a limited energy resource needed for self-control and puzzle solving.
Pragmatism defines truth by its practical consequences and concrete real-world utility.
